raw_case_text:
A 32-year-old male with adjustment and developmental disorders presented with rapidly progressive neurological symptoms and altered consciousness over 10 days, which prompted transport from a preceding hospital. He had no history of prior opportunistic infections. Findings of the systemic evaluation suggested meningitis and led to the diagnosis of pneumonia, for which empirical antibacterial therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin was initiated. Initial serological testing, prompted by his background as a man who has sex with men, was positive for HIV antigen/antibody and syphilis, prompting transfer for suspected acute HIV with neurological complications.
Upon arrival at our hospital, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 13 (eyes, 4; verbal, 3; motor, 6). His vital signs were as follows: respiratory rate, 18 breaths/min on 3-L/min nasal cannula oxygen; peripheral oxygen saturation, 94%; heart rate, 78 beats/min; blood pressure, 136/100 mmHg; and temperature, 36.9 C. Physical examination revealed cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy and nuchal rigidity, suggesting meningeal irritation.
Initial laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 9600/muL, severe lymphopenia (lymphocyte 0.8%; 77 cells/muL), and a subsequent CD4+ count of 5.5%, indicative of profound immunosuppression consistent with advanced HIV/acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). The C-reactive protein level was 1.22 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis showed mild hypoxemia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed high opening pressure (23 cmH2O), low cell count (2 cells/muL), elevated protein level (69 mg/dL), and low glucose level (23 mg/dL). Computed tomography (CT) revealed mild lateral ventricular enlargement and diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, suspicious for pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) (Figure 1). Syphilis and suspected PCP were diagnosed. Due to suspicion of severe pneumocystis pneumonia, empirical therapy with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and aqueous prednisolone was initiated in the emergency room. The treatment of suspected PCP was prioritized, leading to the deliberate delay of induction antifungal therapy despite meningitis concerns and consideration of DC.
  Cryptococcus neoformans  was rapidly identified on CSF analysis on hospital Day 1 (Day 1), leading to a diagnosis of DC. Prompt antifungal therapy (liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine) was subsequently initiated. However, his condition rapidly deteriorated within 10 h. By 18 h, he developed severe hypoxemia (P/F ratio~100), requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. He then sustained two cardiopulmonary arrests, the second necessitating VA-ECMO. The subsequent post-cardiac arrest syndrome was characterized by a no-flow time of 0 min and a low-flow time of a maximum of 17 min. Broad-spectrum antibacterial coverage (meropenem and vancomycin) was initiated for presumed sepsis. The patient also developed severe disseminated intravascular coagulation requiring aggressive transfusion (red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma, ~20 units each on Day 3 due to persistent tracheal bleeding). A CT scan was obtained, which revealed no surgical bleeding source. However, severe hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, splenic infarction, hepatic ischemia, and extensive bilateral atelectasis were observed (Figure 2A-D). Elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin I level, 12,015 pg/dL; creatine kinase-MB level, 245.5 ng/dL) indicated substantial myocardial damage. Echocardiography revealed severely impaired cardiac function (ejection fraction 10%-20%, diffuse hypokinesis, and pericardial effusion). By Day 4, his neurological prognosis was deemed poor, leading to a transition to palliative care. The patient died on Day 6 of hospitalization.
Postmortem examination revealed cryptococcal infiltration within the myocardial interstitium and capillaries, accompanied by microemboli (Figure 3A). Other findings included severe softening of the brainstem and cerebellum (Figure 3B) and organ necrosis, for example, the liver and spleen (Figure 3C,D). Based on the postmortem findings, the final diagnoses included AIDS, DC, and post-cardiac arrest syndrome, likely due to myocardial microemboli from fungal elements and thrombi.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old male presented with a 10-day history of rapidly progressive neurological symptoms and altered consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 10 days prior to transfer, the patient developed rapidly worsening neurological symptoms and decreased consciousness. Evaluation at a preceding hospital suggested meningitis and pneumonia (treated empirically with ceftriaxone and azithromycin) and identified positive HIV antigen/antibody and syphilis serologies, prompting transfer.
subjective.past_medical_history: Adjustment and developmental disorders; man who has sex with men; newly diagnosed HIV and syphilis; no history of prior opportunistic infections.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for altered consciousness and respiratory insufficiency.

objective.physical_examination: Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13 (E4V3M6); vital signs: respiratory rate 18 breaths/min on 3 L/min nasal cannula oxygen (SpO2 94%), heart rate 78 beats/min, blood pressure 136/100 mmHg, temperature 36.9 C. Physical examination revealed cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy and nuchal rigidity.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 9600/uL with severe lymphopenia (0.8%, 77 cells/uL), CRP 1.22 mg/dL, positive HIV Ag/Ab and syphilis serologies, and mild hypoxemia on ABG. Following cardiac arrest on day 1, troponin I was 12,015 pg/dL and CK-MB was 245.5 ng/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell percentage was 5.5%. Initial CT showed mild lateral ventricular enlargement and diffuse bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities. Lumbar puncture revealed opening pressure 23 cmH2O, CSF cell count 2 cells/uL, elevated protein 69 mg/dL, and low glucose 23 mg/dL, with CSF analysis identifying Cryptococcus neoformans on Day 1. Post-arrest CT showed severe hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, splenic infarction, hepatic ischemia, and bilateral atelectasis; echocardiography showed LVEF 10-20% with diffuse hypokinesis and pericardial effusion; autopsy revealed cryptococcal myocardial infiltration and capillary microemboli with brainstem/cerebellar softening and hepatic/splenic necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of advanced HIV/AIDS complicated by fatal disseminated cryptococcosis (meningitis and cryptococcal myocarditis/myocardial microemboli), syphilis, and suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia, confirmed by Day 1 CSF identification of Cryptococcus neoformans and postmortem histopathology showing fungal myocardial infiltration and capillary microemboli. Initially treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisolone for suspected PCP, followed on Day 1 by IV liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine; within 18 hours he suffered severe hypoxemia, two cardiopulmonary arrests requiring VA-ECMO, severe DIC, and multiorgan ischemia, and died on hospital day 6 after transition to palliative care.
